client: I've been really struggling at work lately, and honestly I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything. My team is already short-staffed, and then on top of that they assigned me this huge project with a deadline that feels almost impossible to meet. I just feel like I'm drowning, and no matter how much I do, it never feels like enough.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — the pressure of an understaffed team *plus* an overwhelming project would wear anyone down, and that feeling of "never enough" is genuinely exhausting. I hear your skepticism about whether talking will help, and I think that's worth honoring — change doesn't come from words alone, but sometimes it starts with understanding what's driving that sense of drowning. When you say it never feels like enough, I'm curious — is that a message coming from the situation itself, or is it also something you find yourself believing about *you* personally?

client: Honestly, it's probably both, but I think deep down I do believe it's me — like I should be able to handle this better than I am. I look at my manager and some of my coworkers and they seem to just push through, and I wonder why I can't do the same thing. It makes me feel kind of pathetic, like there's something wrong with me for struggling this much.
therapist: That belief — that struggling means something is *wrong* with you — is such a painful place to be, and I want to gently challenge it: you're comparing your inner experience (the full weight of your exhaustion and doubt) to your coworkers' *outer* appearance, which is rarely the whole picture. Most people who look like they're "pushing through" are quietly struggling too, just in ways you don't get to see. What do you think you would say to a close friend who came to you feeling exactly the way you're feeling right now?

client: I know what you're going to say — that I'd be kind to a friend and tell them they're doing their best, and so I should say that to myself too. And yeah, I guess I would say that to someone else, but it just feels different when it's me, like that logic doesn't quite apply. I don't know why it's so easy to extend grace to other people but when it comes to myself it just feels like making excuses.
therapist: You've actually just named something really important — that extending compassion to yourself *feels* like making excuses, and that distinction is worth exploring, because it tells us something about a rule you might be holding yourself to that you don't apply to others. It's not that the logic doesn't apply to you — it's that somewhere along the way you may have learned that self-compassion is something you have to *earn*, while others deserve it just by virtue of being human. What do you think that says about how you see your own worth compared to the people around you?

client: That's kind of an uncomfortable question to sit with, because I think if I'm being honest, I do see myself as less deserving somehow — like I have to prove my value constantly, especially at work. It's not something I've ever really said out loud before, and hearing it framed that way makes it feel more real and kind of unsettling. I'm not sure how understanding that actually helps me get through this impossible deadline though, you know?
therapist: It takes real courage to say that out loud for the first time, and I want you to know that unsettled feeling is actually a sign something meaningful just shifted — that belief, "I have to constantly prove my value," is likely the very thing making this deadline feel so much more crushing than it might otherwise be. When your worth feels tied to your output, every obstacle becomes a threat to who you *are*, not just what you're doing. So practically speaking, I wonder — if you didn't have to prove anything, what would "good enough" actually look like for this project?

client: That's a really hard question because I genuinely don't know what "good enough" looks like — I think I've been operating in this all-or-nothing mode for so long that anything less than perfect feels like failure. Maybe good enough would be hitting the core deliverables and not killing myself over every small detail, but even as I say that, part of me is already arguing back that if I let myself off the hook, everything will fall apart. I guess I'm scared that "good enough" is just a slippery slope to not caring at all.
therapist: You just articulated something really significant — that "good enough" feels dangerous, like it's one step away from total collapse, and that fear is actually what keeps the all-or-nothing thinking locked in place. But notice what you also said: you *could* define good enough as hitting the core deliverables, which sounds thoughtful and responsible, not careless — that's not someone who stops caring, that's someone learning to care *sustainably*. What evidence do you actually have that letting go of perfectionism in the past has led to things falling apart, versus just feeling uncomfortable?

client: When I actually try to think of specific examples, I'm struggling to come up with a time where things genuinely fell apart because I didn't do something perfectly — it's more like everything just felt really uncomfortable and I was convinced disaster was coming, but it usually didn't. I think I've been confusing that anxious feeling with actual evidence that something went wrong. But it's hard to trust that pattern because the anxiety feels so real and convincing in the moment, like it's warning me about something legitimate.
therapist: You just made a really powerful discovery — that the anxiety has been *masquerading* as evidence, when really it's been a feeling, not a fact, and that distinction matters enormously. The discomfort was real, but it was your nervous system sounding an alarm that never quite matched the actual outcome — and noticing that pattern is exactly how you start to loosen its grip over time. When that anxious warning voice shows up around this deadline, what do you think it would feel like to treat it as *noise to notice* rather than *truth to obey*?

client: I like the idea of that, but I honestly don't know how realistic it is in the middle of a stressful workday when the anxiety just hits full force — it's easy to think about it calmly right now, but in the moment it feels like trying to reason with a fire alarm while the building is burning. I guess I'm worried I'll just revert back to my old patterns the second the pressure ramps up again. How do you actually practice that in real life without it just becoming another thing I feel like I'm failing at?
therapist: Your fire alarm metaphor is perfect, and you're right — we're not aiming for calm reasoning in the middle of the storm, we're aiming for something much smaller, like a brief pause to ask "is this a feeling or a fact?" before you react. The goal isn't perfection at this either — even catching it once out of five times is real progress, and noticing when you *didn't* catch it is data, not failure. So to make it concrete, what's one small moment in your workday — even just a breath before responding to a stressful email — where you could practice that tiny pause?

client: I think the email thing could actually work because there's this automatic reaction I have where I see a message from my manager and my stomach just drops before I've even read it. Maybe I could try taking one breath before I open it, just to create a tiny bit of space. But I'll be honest, part of me is already worried that I'll do it for a day or two and then forget, and then I'll feel guilty about not keeping up with it — which I realize is kind of ironic given everything we just talked about.
therapist: The fact that you caught that irony yourself — that even *this* small practice could become another thing to feel guilty about — shows how much self-awareness you've built just in this conversation. So let's build that safety net in from the start: if you forget for a few days, that's not falling off the wagon, that's just Tuesday, and you simply start again without the guilt tax. What would it mean for you to treat this as an experiment you're curious about rather than a commitment you could fail?

client: Framing it as an experiment actually takes some pressure off, because experiments aren't supposed to have a predetermined right answer — you're just seeing what happens. I think I could maybe get behind that, even if part of me is still a little suspicious that I'm just finding a more sophisticated way to let myself off the hook. I guess what I'm realizing is that a lot of this work is going to happen in those small moments at my desk, not in a therapy session, and that feels both hopeful and kind of lonely honestly.
therapist: That moment of honesty — that it feels lonely — is really touching, and I don't want to gloss over it, because you're right that the real work happens in quiet moments when no one is watching and it's just you and that anxious voice. That loneliness is real, but it's also worth noticing that you're no longer completely alone with these patterns — you're starting to *see* them, name them, and that inner observer you're developing becomes a kind of companion in those moments. What would it feel like to think of that small pause before the email as a moment of showing up *for yourself*, rather than a lonely struggle?

client: That reframe actually got to me a little, because I've never really thought about showing up for myself as something that could happen in a tiny moment like that — I always imagined it would look like some big dramatic act of self-care. I think there's something kind of quietly powerful about the idea that taking one breath before opening an email is actually an act of loyalty to myself, not just a coping trick. I'm still not sure I fully believe I deserve that kind of attention from myself, but I think today I've at least started to question whether that belief is actually true.
therapist: What you just said is genuinely moving — that quiet shift from "I don't deserve this" to "maybe I should question whether that's actually true" is not a small thing, that's the beginning of something real. You came in today skeptical that talking could change anything, and you're leaving with a crack of light in a belief that's been running your life for a long time. I want to ask you to carry one thing with you this week: when you take that breath before the email, can you let it be a small reminder that you're worth that one second of care?
